title: Enzyme kinetics & inhibition
examples: What is the difference between competitive and non-competitive inhibition?
How does the inhibitor affect the Km value?
Can you explain what Vmax represents in this context?

explain.say: Today we look at how enzymes work and how they can be slowed down.
First we learn about Vmax, which is the maximum reaction rate possible.
Next we look at Km, which is the substrate concentration at half Vmax.
Competitive inhibition means the inhibitor blocks the active site directly.
Non-competitive inhibition affects the enzyme structure elsewhere, not the active site.
In a real lab, you might see this when testing drug effectiveness on an enzyme.

draw.text: Real life: Drug action on enzymes

faq.q: What does it mean if Vmax decreases?
faq.a: It means the maximum speed of the reaction has been lowered. This often happens when the enzyme is damaged or blocked.
asks: Why is the maximum rate lower?

faq.q: Does Km change when I add a competitive inhibitor?
faq.a: Yes, the apparent Km increases. This means you need more substrate to reach half the maximum rate.
asks: How does Km relate to substrate concentration?
Does the inhibitor affect Km value?

faq.q: What is the difference between the two types of inhibition?
faq.a: Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind to a different part of the enzyme.

faq.q: If I increase the substrate concentration a lot, what happens?
faq.a: The reaction rate will approach Vmax, regardless of the inhibitor, if the inhibition is competitive.
asks: What is the limit of the reaction rate?

faq.q: Can you explain how the graph helps us tell the difference?
faq.a: The graph changes differently for each type of inhibitor. Competitive changes Km but not Vmax, while non-competitive changes Vmax but not Km.
asks: How do I interpret the Lineweaver-Burk plot?
What does the graph tell us about binding?

facts: Vmax represents the rate when the enzyme is saturated with substrate.
Km is the substrate concentration required for the reaction rate to be half of Vmax.
Competitive inhibitors reversibly bind to the enzyme's active site.
Non-competitive inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site.

quiz.say: If an inhibitor increases the apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, what type of inhibition is occurring?
quiz.why: This pattern shows the inhibitor competing for the active site, making more substrate needed to reach half Vmax.

wrong.1: This would decrease Vmax, not leave it unchanged.
wrong.2: This would decrease both Vmax and Km.
wrong.3: This would mean both Km and Vmax remain the same.

quiz.say: Which type of inhibitor reduces the overall maximum reaction rate, regardless of substrate concentration?
quiz.why: Binding elsewhere reduces the functional enzyme concentration, thus lowering the maximum rate achievable.

wrong.1: This only affects Km, not the ultimate Vmax.
wrong.2: This lowers both Vmax and Km proportionally.
wrong.3: This increases the rate up to Vmax, it does not lower it.

quiz.say: A graph shows the rate is lower at all substrate levels, but the ratio of substrate needed to reach half-rate compared to the uninhibited rate is the same. What is the inhibition type?
quiz.why: If Km is unchanged, the inhibitor does not affect the substrate's affinity for the enzyme.

wrong.0: This would mean the rate is not lower at all substrate levels.
wrong.2: This would change the apparent Km value.
wrong.3: This would change the apparent Km value as well.
